question:
A 68-year-old male presents to urology clinic for follow-up five days after an emergency department
visit for urinary retention, which was managed with a Foley catheter. His medical history includes
hypertension, type II diabetes mellitus, stroke, dyslipidemia, previous myocardial infarction, and severe
right hip osteoarthritis. The patient is poorly compliant with medications and has inadequately
controlled comorbidities. Current evaluation reveals a serum PSA of 6.0 ng/mL (reference range: < 4
ng/mL), and digital rectal examination shows a nontender prostate with multiple rock-hard nodules.
After Foley removal, the patient demonstrates normal urination. What is the most appropriate next step
in management? Answer Choices: (A) Initiation of 5-alpha reductase inhibitor therapy (B) Initiation of
antibiotics for possible prostatitis (C) Cystoscopy to assess for bladder outlet obstruction (D) Immediate
urology referral for radical prostatectomy evaluation (E) Transrectal prostate biopsy (F) Initiation of
alpha-blocker therapy (G) Reassurance (H) Referral for pelvic MRI (I) Observation with periodic DRE
and PSA monitoring (J) Repeat PSA test
 A. Initiation of alpha-blocker therapy
B. Transrectal prostate biopsy

C. Referral for pelvic MRI
D. Observation with periodic DRE and PSA monitoring
E. Reassurance
F. Repeat PSA test
G. Initiation of 5-alpha reductase inhibitor therapy
H. Immediate urology referral for radical prostatectomy evaluation
I. Cystoscopy to assess for bladder outlet obstruction
J. Initiation of antibiotics for possible prostatitis
